screens.title: RDS Reserved Instances (RIs)
screens.narratorSegment: Reserved Instances for Amazon RDS are a commitment-based pricing option that reduce cost for predictable, long-running database workloads. The key idea is simple: if your database runs 24/7 and you can predict the instance class, engine, and deployment configuration, committing to a one- or three-year RI typically produces the largest savings. A concrete example is a production OLTP database that uses a specific instance class and runs continuously; purchasing a three-year RI can provide deep discounts compared to on-demand hourly pricing. A common misconception is that RIs are always the right answer. They are not ideal for development or test databases that are frequently stopped or resized because you keep paying for the reserved capacity even when instances are stopped. Another mistake is mismatching the RI attributes — the engine, Multi-AZ deployment, and instance class should align with usage. Practical steps include auditing usage patterns, matching RI attributes to actual instances, and using partial coverage or regional convertible RIs when some flexibility is needed. Key takeaway: use RIs when utilization is stable and predictable, and avoid them for resources that are often idle or changing shape.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › RDS Reserved Instances
Core Concept

Reserved Instances explained

Commit to 1- or 3-year terms for stable savings when instances run continuously.

Why it matters
  • Significant cost reduction for predictable, always-on databases.
  • Best for production systems with stable instance classes and configurations.
  • Helps finance forecast long-term database expense.
Common mistake
Buying RIs for development databases that are stopped or frequently resized.
Key Takeaway

Use RIs when utilization is stable; audit usage before committing and avoid RIs for volatile or stopped resources.

Practical checklist
  • Record 30–90 days of instance usage to understand baseline.
  • Match RI attributes to engine, instance class, and Multi-AZ if required.
  • Consider regional convertible RIs for flexibility across instance families.
Concrete example
A production OLTP database running db.r5.large 24/7 can save substantially with a 3-year RI versus the hourly on-demand rate.
Misconception check
RIs do not pause billing if instances are stopped. If your instance is stopped or frequently resized, RIs can increase cost rather than reduce it.

screens.title: Aurora Serverless
screens.narratorSegment: Aurora Serverless provides on-demand compute for Aurora databases by automatically starting, stopping, and scaling capacity based on application demand. This model is especially cost-effective for intermittent, spiky, or development workloads that do not justify always-on instances. For example, a development environment that serves internal testing traffic only during business hours can scale to zero during nights and weekends, eliminating the cost of running a base instance. The difference between Aurora Serverless and RIs is a trade-off between predictable low unit cost with commitment and flexible pay-for-what-you-use billing. A common misconception is thinking Serverless always costs less; for sustained high utilization, provisioned instances with RIs will usually be cheaper. Architecturally, use Serverless when you expect large changes in concurrent connections or when you want to avoid instance management. Also consider cold-start implications and connection management strategies in your application. The practical choice should be driven by expected request patterns, cost modeling, and the operational burden you are willing to accept. Aurora Serverless means aurora serverless fits intermittent, unpredictable workloads by billing for actual capacity used, but it can be more expensive for steady, high-utilization systems.. In practical terms, on-demand, auto-scaling compute for intermittent relational workloads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Aurora Serverless
Definition

Aurora Serverless architecture

Automatic start, stop, and capacity scaling for Aurora when demand is variable.

When to choose it
  • Development, test, or infrequently used applications.
  • New projects with unknown traffic where flexibility is valuable.
  • Workloads with short bursts of activity separated by idle periods.
Practical note

For steady high utilization, model costs; Serverless may cost more than reserved provisioned instances.

Concrete example
A staging database that is only active during weekdays can scale to minimal capacity overnight. You pay only for the capacity consumed, removing the need to manage instance sizes or buy RIs for an environment that is not always active.
Misconception check
Serverless removes manual provisioning but does not automatically guarantee lower cost. Compare expected sustained load to Serverless pricing before choosing it for production workloads.
Operational tips
  • Plan for cold-start behavior and connection pooling.
  • Use Serverless where the administrative overhead of instances is a larger cost than runtime price.

screens.title: Right-sizing RDS Instances
screens.narratorSegment: Right-sizing database instances is a continuous process of measuring C P U, memory, and input and output against performance requirements, then selecting the smallest instance class that meets SLAs. Start by collecting 30 to 90 days of metrics to capture typical and peak load. Look for sustained low C P U and memory use, which signals opportunity to downsize. Also inspect input and output patterns: heavy input and output might need a different storage type or larger instance class. A concrete step-by-step process is to identify candidates, run a short-term resize test in a non-production environment to verify performance, and then apply changes with monitoring and a rollback plan. A common misconception is equating low average C P U with safe downsizing — short but critical spikes can be missed by averages, so examine percentiles and peak windows. Right-sizing pairs well with choosing RIs or serverless options: only commit to RIs after you confirm the correct instance family and size. Takeaway: use data-driven experiments, watch percentile metrics, and include input and output and memory in your evaluation, not just C P U.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Right-sizing RDS
Process

Measure → Test → Validate → Commit

  1. Collect 30–90 days of CPU, memory, and I/O metrics including percentiles.
  2. Identify candidates with sustained low utilization for downsizing.
  3. Run resize tests in staging that reproduce peak load.
  4. Monitor SLAs, and if satisfied, apply change with a rollback plan.
Example scenario
A database with average CPU at 10% but periodic spikes at 70% in short windows should be assessed by 95th percentile metrics. If spikes are brief, downsizing may still be safe; if spikes align with business-critical jobs, maintain headroom.
Pitfalls
  • Relying on averages hides peak behavior.
  • Ignoring I/O or memory requirements when picking instance families.
Key Takeaway

Use percentile metrics and validate with tests before committing to a long-term purchase.

screens.title: DynamoDB Capacity Modes
screens.narratorSegment: DynamoDB offers two capacity modes: Provisioned Capacity, where you set read and write throughput units, and On-Demand Capacity, which charges per request. Provisioned is cost-effective when you have predictable traffic and can tune RCUs and WCUs, especially at scale. On-Demand simplifies management because it scales automatically and bills per request, which is great for unpredictable or new applications with potential spikes. A practical example: a startup launching a new app with unknown user patterns gains operational simplicity from On-Demand because it eliminates capacity planning and the risk of throttling. Conversely, a high-volume steady workload will usually be cheaper when carefully provisioned and paired with Auto Scaling. A common mistake is assuming On-Demand is always safer; for long-running, high-throughput workloads, it can cost more. The decision requires analyzing access patterns, expected peak-to-average ratios, and operational overhead. We'll use a quick decision heuristic: choose Provisioned when you can predict sustained load and benefit from lower per-unit pricing; choose On-Demand when traffic is unpredictable or cost of being wrong is high. DynamoDB Capacity Modes means use on-demand for unpredictability and rapid launches; use provisioned with auto scaling for predictable, high-volume workloads to minimize unit cost.. In practical terms, provisioned vs on-demand — match mode to traffic patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › DynamoDB Capacity Modes
Provisioned Capacity

Set RCUs & WCUs, use Auto Scaling

Good for predictable workloads. Configure Auto Scaling to adjust provisioned capacity and avoid over-provisioning.

  • Lower unit cost at scale.
  • Requires forecasting and monitoring.
  • Auto Scaling mitigates bursts but needs tuning.
On-Demand Capacity

Pay-per-request

Ideal for unpredictable or spiky workloads and early-stage products. Eliminates capacity planning.

Example
A new mobile app launch where traffic may spike unpredictably — On-Demand avoids throttling or manual scaling.
Misconception check
On-Demand adds operational simplicity but may be more expensive for stable, high-throughput applications.

screens.title: DynamoDB Auto Scaling & Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Auto Scaling for DynamoDB adjusts provisioned RCUs and WCUs in response to traffic, smoothing capacity changes and avoiding manual intervention. The correct configuration begins with realistic target utilization, typically a percentage that balances cost and headroom — for example, 70–80 percent of provisioned capacity — then setting minimum and maximum capacity boundaries to prevent runaway costs or throttling. Start by analyzing traffic patterns to define realistic min/max values and a utilization target. Test scaling with synthetic load and monitor for scaling lag or throttling events. A practical example: if you see daily spikes at noon, set a target that allows Auto Scaling to add capacity quickly before peak and remove it afterward. Watch out for cascading misconfigurations: setting the minimum too high defeats cost savings, while a very low minimum can cause throttling during sudden spikes. Also consider using adaptive capacity features and DynamoDB Accelerator for read-heavy workloads. The final tip is to pair Auto Scaling with robust monitoring and alerts so you can adjust thresholds based on observed behavior. DynamoDB Auto Scaling & Best Practices means set realistic utilization targets, min/max bounds, and test under load to prevent throttling or unnecessary cost growth.. In practical terms, how to configure auto scaling and avoid capacity pitfalls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Process

Configure Auto Scaling with realistic targets

Define utilization targets and bounds, then test and monitor to tune behavior.

Step 1: Analyze traffic
Collect hourly and percentile metrics to understand normal and peak patterns.
Step 2: Set targets
Choose a utilization target (70–80%) and min/max capacity to constrain costs and performance.
Step 3: Test under load
Simulate spikes to confirm scaling responsiveness and absence of throttling.
Step 4: Monitor & tune
Use alarms on throttling, read/write capacity usage, and adjust as traffic evolves.
Tip: Pair Auto Scaling with adaptive capacity and consider DAX for read-heavy workloads to reduce overall RCU usage.

CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE IF NOT EXISTS sales_db.sales_data (

)
ROW FORMAT SERDE 'org.apache.hadoop.hive.serde2.OpenCSVSerde'

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we focus on practical ways to reduce cost across managed databases and analytics services. You will learn how to match workload patterns to payment models — for example, when long-running production databases benefit from Reserved Instances and when bursty or intermittent workloads are better served by serverless options like Aurora Serverless or DynamoDB On-Demand. We'll also look at analytics patterns: how Athena and Redshift Spectrum let you pay for the data scanned rather than for fixed compute, and why data formats and partitioning matter to query cost. Finally, we'll review Glue DPU sizing and operational checks for idle or underutilized resources. A concrete example you will carry through the hands-on section is creating a DynamoDB table in On-Demand mode and querying S3 data with Athena while observing the data-scanned metric. Throughout, we'll highlight common mistakes such as buying RIs for stopped development databases and querying raw CSVs without partitioning. By the end you will be able to pick the most cost-effective configuration for relational, NoSQL, and analytics workloads and explain the trade-offs to stakeholders.

This lesson is focused on four practical skills you will develop. First, you will learn to optimize RDS and Aurora costs by using Reserved Instances when workloads are predictable, or Aurora Serverless for intermittent demand. I will show a concrete example of when a one- or three-year commitment makes sense and the common mistake of applying RIs to stopped development databases. Second, you will implement cost-effective DynamoDB strategies, selecting between On-Demand and Provisioned capacity and configuring Auto Scaling for steady workloads. I'll explain a scenario where On-Demand reduces operational overhead for a new product launch. Third, you will design analytics solutions with Athena and Redshift Spectrum to query S3 directly and reduce infrastructure costs; we'll discuss why columnar formats and partitioning reduce the amount of data scanned. Fourth, you will manage AWS Glue costs by right-sizing DPUs, optimizing scripts to avoid unnecessary shuffles, and scheduling jobs effectively. Each objective ends with a verified competency milestone so you can show you applied the technique in a hands-on activity.

On this complementary objectives slide I'll frame each objective as a practical task and show why it matters in real operations. For RDS and Aurora, the practical task is to calculate expected utilization and decide whether a Reserved Instance fits a 1- or 3-year commitment, or whether Aurora Serverless is preferable for unpredictable test environments. For DynamoDB, you will create a table in On-Demand mode and observe cost per request versus projected Provisioned capacity with Auto Scaling for a steady traffic scenario. For analytics, the task is to run Athena queries against S3 and measure the data scanned metric before and after converting files to Parquet and adding partitions. For Glue, you will run a sample ETL job, adjust DPUs, and compare run time and cost. Each task is designed to create measurable comparisons so you can demonstrate saved cost or reduced manual effort, and avoid common mistakes like assigning RIs to non-production instances or querying unpartitioned CSVs that needlessly increase cost.

Reserved Instances for Amazon RDS are a commitment-based pricing option that reduce cost for predictable, long-running database workloads. The key idea is simple: if your database runs 24/7 and you can predict the instance class, engine, and deployment configuration, committing to a one- or three-year RI typically produces the largest savings. A concrete example is a production OLTP database that uses a specific instance class and runs continuously; purchasing a three-year RI can provide deep discounts compared to on-demand hourly pricing. A common misconception is that RIs are always the right answer. They are not ideal for development or test databases that are frequently stopped or resized because you keep paying for the reserved capacity even when instances are stopped. Another mistake is mismatching the RI attributes — the engine, Multi-AZ deployment, and instance class should align with usage. Practical steps include auditing usage patterns, matching RI attributes to actual instances, and using partial coverage or regional convertible RIs when some flexibility is needed. Key takeaway: use RIs when utilization is stable and predictable, and avoid them for resources that are often idle or changing shape.

Aurora Serverless provides on-demand compute for Aurora databases by automatically starting, stopping, and scaling capacity based on application demand. This model is especially cost-effective for intermittent, spiky, or development workloads that do not justify always-on instances. For example, a development environment that serves internal testing traffic only during business hours can scale to zero during nights and weekends, eliminating the cost of running a base instance. The difference between Aurora Serverless and RIs is a trade-off between predictable low unit cost with commitment and flexible pay-for-what-you-use billing. A common misconception is thinking Serverless always costs less; for sustained high utilization, provisioned instances with RIs will usually be cheaper. Architecturally, use Serverless when you expect large changes in concurrent connections or when you want to avoid instance management. Also consider cold-start implications and connection management strategies in your application. The practical choice should be driven by expected request patterns, cost modeling, and the operational burden you are willing to accept. Aurora Serverless means aurora serverless fits intermittent, unpredictable workloads by billing for actual capacity used, but it can be more expensive for steady, high-utilization systems.. In practical terms, on-demand, auto-scaling compute for intermittent relational workloads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Right-sizing database instances is a continuous process of measuring C P U, memory, and input and output against performance requirements, then selecting the smallest instance class that meets SLAs. Start by collecting 30 to 90 days of metrics to capture typical and peak load. Look for sustained low C P U and memory use, which signals opportunity to downsize. Also inspect input and output patterns: heavy input and output might need a different storage type or larger instance class. A concrete step-by-step process is to identify candidates, run a short-term resize test in a non-production environment to verify performance, and then apply changes with monitoring and a rollback plan. A common misconception is equating low average C P U with safe downsizing — short but critical spikes can be missed by averages, so examine percentiles and peak windows. Right-sizing pairs well with choosing RIs or serverless options: only commit to RIs after you confirm the correct instance family and size. Takeaway: use data-driven experiments, watch percentile metrics, and include input and output and memory in your evaluation, not just C P U.

DynamoDB offers two capacity modes: Provisioned Capacity, where you set read and write throughput units, and On-Demand Capacity, which charges per request. Provisioned is cost-effective when you have predictable traffic and can tune RCUs and WCUs, especially at scale. On-Demand simplifies management because it scales automatically and bills per request, which is great for unpredictable or new applications with potential spikes. A practical example: a startup launching a new app with unknown user patterns gains operational simplicity from On-Demand because it eliminates capacity planning and the risk of throttling. Conversely, a high-volume steady workload will usually be cheaper when carefully provisioned and paired with Auto Scaling. A common mistake is assuming On-Demand is always safer; for long-running, high-throughput workloads, it can cost more. The decision requires analyzing access patterns, expected peak-to-average ratios, and operational overhead. We'll use a quick decision heuristic: choose Provisioned when you can predict sustained load and benefit from lower per-unit pricing; choose On-Demand when traffic is unpredictable or cost of being wrong is high. DynamoDB Capacity Modes means use on-demand for unpredictability and rapid launches; use provisioned with auto scaling for predictable, high-volume workloads to minimize unit cost.. In practical terms, provisioned vs on-demand — match mode to traffic patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Auto Scaling for DynamoDB adjusts provisioned RCUs and WCUs in response to traffic, smoothing capacity changes and avoiding manual intervention. The correct configuration begins with realistic target utilization, typically a percentage that balances cost and headroom — for example, 70–80 percent of provisioned capacity — then setting minimum and maximum capacity boundaries to prevent runaway costs or throttling. Start by analyzing traffic patterns to define realistic min/max values and a utilization target. Test scaling with synthetic load and monitor for scaling lag or throttling events. A practical example: if you see daily spikes at noon, set a target that allows Auto Scaling to add capacity quickly before peak and remove it afterward. Watch out for cascading misconfigurations: setting the minimum too high defeats cost savings, while a very low minimum can cause throttling during sudden spikes. Also consider using adaptive capacity features and DynamoDB Accelerator for read-heavy workloads. The final tip is to pair Auto Scaling with robust monitoring and alerts so you can adjust thresholds based on observed behavior.
